subject: physics_2
question_text: Give a brief account of Thomson model of atom. What are its limitations?

mark_split.label: It cannot explain the line spectra

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. The book prints "the enitre mass", "uniformly distributed" and "(Water milon model)"; the misspellings are corrected here to "entire" and "watermelon model", and the wording is otherwise unchanged. Physics hand-checked: Thomson's atom is a sphere of positive charge about 10⁻¹⁰ m across with the electrons inside it, the electron charge exactly balancing the positive charge; its three recorded failures are the stability of the atom, the large-angle α-scattering Geiger and Marsden measured, and the discrete line spectra of hydrogen and other atoms. FIGURE NOTE: the renderer draws outlines only, with no fills and no occlusion, so the plum pudding is drawn as a sphere OUTLINE with five small electron circles set well apart inside it — not as a shaded sphere with dots laid over it.

recall_prompt: Describe Thomson's model of the atom, then give its three limitations.

steps.label: Thomson's model
lines: Thomson model of atom:
An atom is a positively charged sphere of
radius about 10⁻¹⁰ m. The entire mass and the
positive charge of the atom are spread evenly
through this sphere, and the negative electrons
are placed inside it.
The number of electrons is such that their
negative charge equals the positive charge of
the sphere, so the atom is electrically
neutral.
It is called the plum pudding model, or the
watermelon model.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Sphere size, charge spread evenly, electrons inside, atom neutral.
steps.why: The picture matters: the positive charge fills the whole atom rather than sitting at a point. That is exactly the feature Rutherford's scattering experiment later ruled out.
common_mistakes: Putting the positive charge at the centre. In Thomson's model it fills the whole sphere.
Leaving out the neutrality. The electron charge balancing the positive charge is part of the model.

recall.must_convey: That the atom is a positively charged sphere about 10⁻¹⁰ m across with electrons inside it, and is neutral overall.
reject: it could not explain the line spectra

steps.memory_tip: One positive sphere with electrons set inside it, and no nucleus.

steps.label: The plum pudding model
steps.margin_note: One large circle for the sphere of positive matter, five small circles inside it for the electrons, two leader lines to the labels.
steps.why: The sphere is the positive matter and the small circles are the electrons set inside it. Five is enough to show the arrangement; the real number is whatever makes the atom neutral.
common_mistakes: Drawing the electrons on the surface of the sphere. They sit inside the positive matter.

recall.must_convey: That a large circle is drawn for the positive sphere with small circles inside it for the electrons.
accept: draw a big circle with small circles inside
sphere of positive charge with electrons in it
reject: draw a nucleus at the centre

steps.memory_tip: One big circle, small circles inside, no nucleus anywhere.

steps.label: No stable atom
lines: Limitations:
1. It could not provide stability to the atom.
The positive and negative charges are at rest,
so they would be drawn towards each other and
the separate charges would be destroyed.
Later work showed that the positive and
negative charges in an atom stay as separate
entities, although the atom as a whole is
neutral.
steps.margin_note: First limitation. Charges at rest attract, so nothing holds the arrangement apart.
steps.why: In Thomson's picture nothing keeps the electron away from the positive matter — there is no orbit and no motion. Static opposite charges simply move together, so the model gives no reason for an atom to last.
common_mistakes: Saying the electrons radiate and spiral in. That is Rutherford's problem; Thomson's electrons are not orbiting.
Leaving out the reason. The mark is for the charges being drawn together.

recall.must_convey: That the model gives no stable atom because the positive and negative charges at rest would be drawn together.
accept: could not provide stability to the atom
the charges would be drawn towards each other

steps.memory_tip: Nothing moves, so nothing keeps the charges apart.

steps.label: No large-angle scattering
lines: 2. It could not explain the large angle
scattering of α-particles that pass close to
the atom.
A charge spread thinly through the whole atom
gives only a weak force, so no α-particle
should be turned through a large angle. In the
experiment some were turned back through 180°.
steps.margin_note: Second limitation. Spread-out charge means a weak force, but large deflections were measured.
steps.why: This is the observation that ended the model. A force strong enough to turn a fast α-particle right around needs the positive charge packed into a very small volume, which is what led Rutherford to the nucleus.
common_mistakes: Saying the model predicts no scattering at all. It predicts small-angle scattering only.
Leaving out the reason. Spread-out charge gives a weak force.

recall.must_convey: That the model cannot explain the large-angle scattering of α-particles, because a spread-out charge gives only a weak force.
accept: could not explain large angle scattering
alpha particles passing close to the atom
spread out charge gives a weak force
reject: could not explain the line spectra

steps.memory_tip: Thin charge, weak push — but some α-particles came straight back.

steps.label: No line spectra
lines: 3. It could not explain the presence of discrete
spectral lines emitted by hydrogen and other
atoms. The model has no separate energy levels,
so it gives no reason for a set of fixed
wavelengths.
steps.margin_note: Third limitation, and the box lists all three together.
steps.why: Discrete lines need discrete energy levels. Thomson's sphere has no levels at all, so any radiation from it would be a continuous band, not the sharp lines that are measured.
common_mistakes: Naming only one or two limitations. The question asks for the limitations, so give all three.
Saying the model explains the spectra of hydrogen only. It explains no line spectrum.

recall.must_convey: That the model cannot explain the discrete spectral lines of hydrogen and other atoms.
accept: could not explain the discrete spectral lines
no energy levels in the model
line spectra of hydrogen and other atoms
reject: the charges would be drawn together

steps.memory_tip: Three failures in order: stability, scattering, spectrum.

insider_note: The model is worth one mark and the three limitations one each — number them, because an unnumbered paragraph makes the examiner hunt for the third.
